Umbrella peoples

Maya

Maya is a broad route connecting many living peoples, languages and communities across Mesoamerica and beyond. Archaeology, a contemporary Maya organization and research on forest gardening offer different educational perspectives; none replaces an individual community’s history.

Read the sources [1] Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian [3] Robert Sharer / Penn Museum, Expedition [4] International Maya League

Relief with enthroned ruler, Chakalte’,770 CE
Chakalte’, Relief with enthroned ruler,770 CE, La Pasadita, Guatemala. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, The Michael C. Rockefeller Memorial Collection, Bequest of Nelson A. Rockefeller,1979, object 1979.206.1047. Open Access / CC0.

Source & image record ↗ · Public Domain / Met Open Access CC0

One Classic-period Maya royal artwork from La Pasadita, Guatemala, signed by the named sculptor Chakalte’. Connected only to the broad historical Maya route, not assigned to Itza’, Mopan, Q’eqchi’ or modern Yucatec communities. No present identity, membership, universal design or government endorsement inferred. Complete delivered 1188×1200 source frame viewed; black surrounding field is part of the delivered image.

01

Identity and homelands

Maya is an umbrella identity encompassing many living peoples, languages, communities, and political histories across Mesoamerica.

Read the sources [1] Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian

02

Historical context

Smithsonian’s Living Maya Time connects ancient intellectual traditions with present-day Maya voices, rather than treating Maya history as a vanished civilization.

Read the sources [1] Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian

03

Living communities and further study

ALMG’s community directory opens routes to specific language communities. Study Itza’, Ixil, Mam, K’iche’, Mopan, and other peoples separately as well.

Read the sources [2] Academia de las Lenguas Mayas de Guatemala

04

Many communities and historical polities

Robert Sharer’s archaeological overview distinguishes Preclassic, Classic and Postclassic histories and multiple independent kingdoms. It also warns that elite monuments dominate the surviving written evidence. The fall of particular cities or courts should not be read as disappearance of Maya peoples.

Read the sources [3] Robert Sharer / Penn Museum, Expedition

05

A living organizational voice

The International Maya League describes cultural transmission, intergenerational work and connections across borders as organizational priorities. These are its stated aims, not proof of measured outcomes or a claim that one organization speaks for every Maya community.

Read the sources [4] International Maya League

06

Crops within a managed forest cycle

UCSB’s MesoAmerican Research Center describes milpa as intercropping connected to managed regrowth and forest gardening. Its model directs attention to a changing landscape rather than only to a freshly planted field. Local farming histories and conditions require separate study.

Read the sources [5] University of California Santa Barbara, MesoAmerican Research Center

07

An individually named artist

James Doyle’s Met essay identifies Chakalte’ as the sculptor of a limestone relief from La Pasadita, dated around770 CE. The work belongs to a particular royal setting associated with Yaxchilan. It is presented here as one historical artwork, rather than a motif shared by all Maya communities.

Read the sources [6] James Doyle, 2015 / Metropolitan Museum of Art
